'''''Ixora coccinea''''' (also known as '''jungle geranium''', '''flame of the woods''' or '''jungle flame''' or '''pendkuli''') is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Rubiaceae]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Ixora%20red.html|title=Ixora coccinea catalog|publisher=Flowers of India|access-date=5 July 2015}}</ref> It is a common flowering [[shrub]] native to [[Southern India]], [[Bangladesh]], and [[Sri Lanka]]. It has become one of the most popular flowering shrubs in [[South Florida]] [[garden]]s and [[landscape]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.toxicologycentre.com/English/plants/Botanical/techi.html|title=Ixora coccinea Linn|publisher=Toxicology Center|access-date=5 July 2015|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150705150339/http://www.toxicologycentre.com/English/plants/Botanical/techi.html|archivedate=5 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=no_name12 |date=2022-02-15 |title=40 Florida Shrubs (Flowering, Evergreen, Vines): Pictures and Identification |url=https://leafyplace.com/florida-shrubs/ |access-date=2022-08-01 |website=Leafy Place |language=en-US}}</ref> It is the [[national flower]] of [[Suriname]].{{citation needed|date=April 2019}}

==Description==
[[File:Ixora coccinea Pink INDIA (3).jpg|thumb|left|A pink Ixora coccinea in India]]
''Ixora coccinea'' is a dense, multi-branched [[evergreen]] [[shrub]], commonly {{convert|4–6|ft|m|abbr=on}} in height, but capable of reaching up to {{convert|12|ft|m|abbr=on}} high. It has a rounded form, with a spread that may exceed its height. The [[glossy]], leathery, [[rectangle|oblong]] [[leaves]] are about {{convert|4|in|cm|abbr=on}} long, with entire margins, and are carried in opposite pairs or whorled on the [[Plant stem|stems]]. Small tubular, [[Scarlet (color)|scarlet]] flowers in dense rounded clusters {{convert|2-5|in|cm|abbr=on}} across are produced almost all year long.

==Cultivation and use==
[[File:Jungle geranium seeds @ Kanjirappally, Kerala 02.JPG|thumb|left|150px|Fruits]]
Although there are around 500 [[species]] in the genus ''[[Ixora]]'', only a handful are commonly cultivated, and the common name, Ixora, is usually used for ''I. coccinea''. ''I. coccinea'' is used in [[Temperature|warm]] [[climates]] for [[Hedge (barrier)|hedges]] and screens, foundation plantings, massed in flowering beds, or grown as a [[Biological specimen|specimen]] shrub or small tree. In cooler climate, it is grown in a [[greenhouse]] or as a potted house plant requiring bright light. ''I. coccinea'' is also grown in containers, looking very distinguished as a patio or poolside plant. This tight, compact shrub is much branched and tolerates hard pruning, making it ideal for formal hedges, although it is at its best when not sheared.

[[File:Ixora coccinea Blanco1.21.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Illustration by [[Manuel Blanco Ramos]]]]There are numerous named [[cultivar]]s differing in flower colour ([[yellow]], [[pink]], [[Orange (colour)|orange]]) and plant size. Several popular cultivars are dwarfs, usually staying under {{convert|3|ft|m|abbr=on}} in height. ''Nora Grant'' is a popular dwarf and ''Super King'' is a popular [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] with much larger [[flower]] clusters. Many new cultivars and hybrids of ''I. coccinea'' have come to market in the last couple of decades, leading to a resurgence in popularity for the beautiful flame-of-the-woods.
[[File:Ixora coccinea (flame of the woods).jpg|thumb|Ixora coccinea at Bui National Park in Ghana]]
The flowers, leaves, roots, and the stem are used to treat various ailments in the Indian traditional system of medicine, the [[Ayurveda]], and in various folk medicines, in traditional Indian medicine the fusion of juice leaves and the fruit of Ixora coccinea is used to care for dysentery, ulcers and gonorrhea.

==Chemical constituents==
Phytochemical studies indicate that the plant contains the phytochemicals [[lupeol]], [[ursolic acid]], [[oleanolic acid]], [[sitosterol]], [[rutin]], [[lecocyanadin]], [[anthocyanin]]s, [[proanthocyanidin]]s, and [[glycoside]]s of [[kaempferol]] and [[quercetin]].<ref>Baliga MS, Kurian PJ "Ixora coccinea Linn.: traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacology",  Chin J Integr Med. 2012 Jan;18(1):72-9</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Ixora coccinea'' was first described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his ''[[Species Plantarum]] 1: 110''.<ref>[http://www.tropicos.org/Name/27900204 ''Ixora coccinea'' en Trópicos]</ref>
